review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Conventional rechargeable zinc-air batteries (ZABs) face two critical challenges: (1) slow
kinetics of the oxygen reduction (ORR) and oxygen evolution (OER) reactions; and (2) the
thermodynamic incompatibility of OER and ORR occurring concurrently on a single air cathode.
To address these limitations, we propose in this study a dual-cathode zinc-ethylene glycol/air
battery (D-ZEAB) that spatially decouples ORR and the ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR)
onto separate cathodes, enabling concurrent electricity generation and electroreforming of
polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic waste into high-value C chemicals. Furthermore, we
develop a bifunctional catalyst composed of defect- rich subnanometer-thick PdCuCo trimetallenes
to enhance both EGOR and ORR kinetics. Benefiting from the decoupled cathode configuration
and the bifunctional PdCuCo catalyst, the D-ZEAB demonstrates an energy conversion efficiency
of 91.7%, a long cycle life of 1696 h, and a Faradaic efficiency of >93% for GA production. This
work not only presents a promising strategy for advancing the zinc-air battery technology but also
offers a sustainable route for simultaneous energy storage and plastic waste upcycling.

---

## Introduction

Energy shortage and environmental pollution remain persistent global challenges, driving
the development of sustainable energy storage systems such as metal-air batteries, metal-ion
batteries, metal-sulfur batteries, and fuel cells.1, 2, 3, 4 Among them, rechargeable zinc-air batteries
(ZABs) utilizing atmospheric oxygen as the cathode active substance are widely considered
promising energy storage and conversion devices due to their high theoretical energy density (1350
Wh kg-1), cost-effectiveness, and environmental benignity.5, 6 A typical ZAB consists of a zinc
anode, an aqueous electrolyte, and a bifunctional air cathode that facilitates oxygen reduction
(ORR) during discharge and oxygen evolution (OER) during charge.7, 8 However, the
commercialization of ZABs remains hindered by several limitations: (1) the absence of cost-
effective bifunctional electrocatalysts that can enhance the sluggish ORR and OER kinetics leads
to low per-cycle capacity, large charging/discharging voltage gaps (∆E), and reduced energy
conversion efficiency; (2) the single-cathode configuration requires both ORR and OER to occur
on the same electrode, which, due to their opposing thermodynamic requirements, accelerates
catalyst oxidation and deactivation, thus reducing the discharging capacity and cycle life of the
batteries; (3) the charging process produces low-value oxygen, which undermines the economic
viability of ZABs. Thus, strategies to improve the energy efficiency, economic efficiency, and
operational stability of ZABs are urgently needed.

Recently, a class of zinc-X/air hybrid batteries (ZXAHBs, X = KI, alcohol, or urea) has been
proposed, wherein the kinetically sluggish OER is replaced with thermodynamically favorable
oxidation reactions (XOR) involving readily oxidizable substances, such as KI, alcohol, and urea.9,
10, 11, 12 These hybrid batteries demonstrate a significant improvement in energy conversion
efficiency by lowering the required charging voltages. However, despite their enhanced charging
performance, challenges persist, including: the unresolved thermodynamic mismatch between
ORR and XOR on a single air cathode; the absence of highly active and selective bifunctional
catalysts for both ORR and XOR; the low economic value of products generated during the battery
charging process (e.g., N from urea oxidation, and CO from most alcohol oxidations);11, 13, 14 and
2 2
the potential battery safety hazards arising from the introduction of flammable organic compounds
(e.g., methanol, ethanol) into the electrolyte. As a result, most reported ZXAHBs demonstrate only
modest performance, with areal discharging capacities ≤ 2 mAh cm-2 per cycle and cycle lifetimes
≤ 400 h.15, 16 To meet the demands of large-scale commercialization, zinc-air and hybrid batteries
must overcome these kinetic and thermodynamic limitations, achieving high areal capacity, energy
conversion efficiency, product selectivity, and long -term stability.

In this work, we introduce a dual-cathode zinc-ethylene glycol/air battery (D-ZEAB) that
spatially decouples the ORR and ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR) onto separate
cathodes. This design enables simultaneous electricity generation and electroreforming of PET
plastic waste into high-value C chemicals. By isolating the two reactions, the D-ZEAB optimizes
2
the thermodynamic conditions for EGOR (charging) and ORR (discharging), while preventing the
oxidation of ORR catalyst. Thereby, the discharging capacity and cycle life are both enhanced.
Moreover, replacing OER with the thermodynamically favorable EGOR significantly reduces
charging voltages and improves energy conversion efficiency. From a kinetic perspective, efficient
catalysts with low overpotentials for ethylene glycol-to-glycolic acid oxidation and the ORR are
required to enable high-performance operation of D-ZEAB. While Pd exhibits high activity for
both EGOR and ORR, its practical application is hindered by challenges in atomic utilization, mass
activity, and stability.17, 18 Integrating alloying and structure engineering to design Pd-based
trimetallene aims to retain high atomic utilization via quantum size effect and synergistically
optimize EGOR/ORR performance through ternary component interactions and tailored
architectures. Therefore, defect-rich PdCuCo trimetallene was further engineered as dual-cathode
catalyst to accelerate EGOR/ORR kinetics. Leveraging synergistic structural (e.g., lattice defects,
compressive strain, and metallene architecture) and alloying effects, the optimized PdCuCo-0.9
achieves high electrocatalytic performance: an EGOR mass activity of 16.6 A mg -1, an ORR half-
Pd
wave potential of 0.90 V (vs. RHE), and notable durability. In situ experiments and density
functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the synergistic structural and alloying effects
modulate the electronic structure of Pd sites on PdCuCo. This modulation weakens the adsorption
of the carbonyl (*CO) intermediate intermediate and accelerates the in situ formation of Pd-O(H)
ad
species, thereby facilitating the selective oxidation from ethylene glycol to glycolic acid (GA).
As a result of the decoupled cathode configuration and the notable bifunctional catalytic activity,
the
PdCuCo-based D-ZEAB achieves an energy density of 868 Wh kg-1, a discharging capacity of 10
mAh per cycle, and a long cycle life of 1696 h, with a Faradaic efficiency exceeding 93% for GA
production. Notably, the battery retains a high energy conversion efficiency of 91.7% even after
1696 h of continuous cycling.

---

## Results

Design and working principle of rechargeable D-ZEAB
Fig. 1a schematically illustrates the configuration and working mechanism of the
rechargeable D-ZEAB. The battery features four key components: (1) a porous zinc anode; (2) a
charging cathode utilizing PET hydrolysate solution as electrolyte; (3) a discharging cathode with
6.0 M KOH+0.2 M Zn(OAc) mixed electrolyte; and (4) a membrane separating the two
2
electrolytes. This spatially decoupled cathode configuration enables the ORR and EGOR to
proceed independently under their respective optimal thermodynamic conditions without
interfering with each other. During operation, the system automatically switches between two
modes: charging (EGOR at one cathode to produce high-value GA) and discharging (ORR at the
other cathode). The detailed reaction pathways and the thermodynamic calculations provided in
Supplementary Eqs. S1-S9. Unlike conventional ZABs that are limited by the sluggish OER, the
charging process of D-ZEAB is significantly optimized by the low oxidation potential (~0.2 V vs.
SHE) and fast kinetics of EGOR.19 Theoretical calculations indicate that the D-ZEAB achieves an
low charging voltage of ~0.623 V (Supplementary Eqs. S9), representing a reduction of at least
1.030 V compared to typical ZABs (Fig. 1b). Additionally, the decoupled cathode design prevents
the oxidation-induced deactivation of ORR catalyst even at high charging voltages, dramatically
enhancing the cycle stability. Notably, the system also offers compelling sustainability advantages:
ethylene glycol (key EGOR reactant) can be abundantly sourced from PET waste hydrolysis,
creating a circular economy.20, 21 Beyond electricity generation during the discharging process, the
D-ZEAB simultaneously produces valuable GA through electroreforming of PET plastic waste.
As shown in Fig. 1c, this integrated approach presents a more cost-effective, energy-efficient, and
environmentally benign alternative to conventional GA production methods, offering significant
potential for addressing global plastic pollution while advancing energy storage technology.

Synthesis and characterization of PdCuCo trimetallenes
To achieve high-efficiency operation of the D-ZEAB, we developed defect-rich PdCuCo
trimetallenes as advanced bifunctional catalysts for simultaneous EGOR and ORR enhancement
(Fig. 2a). The catalysts were synthesized via a one-pot solvothermal method using Pd2+, Cu2+ and
Co2+ precursors with ethylenediamine (EDA) as the reducing agent. The X-ray diffraction (XRD)
analysis of PdCuCo trimetallenes confirms the formation of well-alloyed face-centered cubic (fcc)
phases (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. S1). The diffraction peaks of PdCuCo trimetallenes are
positively shifted compared to pure Pd, indicating the existence of lattice compression due to the
incorporation of Cu/Co with a smaller atomic radius into the Pd lattice. Meanwhile, the broadened
diffraction peaks of PdCuCo trimetallenes suggest reduced crystallite size and the generation of
lattice defects caused by Cu/Co incorporation.22 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and
inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) results verify the
coexistence of Pd, Cu, and Co elements, with a bulk composition of Pd/Cu/Co = 55.0/44.1/0.9 for
PdCuCo-0.9 (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Table S1). High-resolution transmission electron
microscopy (HR-TEM) observations reveal a 2D sheet-like morphology of PdCuCo-0.9 with an
average lateral size of ~20 nm (Fig. 2d and 2e); and atomic force microscopy (AFM) analyses
further verify a metallene structure of PdCuCo -0.9 (~1.0 nm thickness, ~5 atomic layers;
Supplementary Fig. S2). The sub-nanometer metallene architecture is conducive to shortening
diffusion pathways for reactant/intermediate and enhancing mass/charge transfer efficiency during
the electrocatalysis process. The combined structural and compositional features synergistically
contribute to the catalyst's high performance in the D-ZEAB system.23

Atomic-scale lattice configuration of PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene was investigated using
aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM). As denoted
by the blue dashed circles in Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. S3, numerous lattice distortions (LDs)
can be observed in PdCuCo-0.9, arising from the atomic size mismatch between Pd, Cu, and Co
constituents. Distinct zigzag atomic steps appear along the curved edges (indicated by red arrows,
Fig. 2g), while the enlarged HAADF-STEM observations further confirm the presence of twin
boundaries (TBs), atomic vacancies (AVs), and stacking faults (SFs) (Fig. 2h-2j). These structural
defects are expected to modulate the surface electronic states and enhance the electrocatalytic
activity.24 The integrated pixel intensities obtained by line-scan along the [111] direction reveal an
average lattice spacing of 2.22 Å for (111) planes (Fig. 2k). This represents an approximately 6.3%
compressive strain in PdCuCo-0.9 relative to the bulk Pd crystal (2.30 Å, JCPDS No. 87-0637),
attributed to atomic size difference and lattice defects.25 EDS mapping further validates
homogenous distribution of Pd, Cu, and Co elements throughout the nanostructure (Fig. 2l and
2m). To assess the impacts of Cu and Co incorporation, control samples including PdCuCo-0.3,
PdCuCo-1.7, PdCu alloy, and monometallic Pd were also synthesized using the same approach.
The representative TEM and EDS elemental mapping images of these control samples reveal
similar lattice defects across these variants (Supplementary Fig. S4-S6), which underscores the
versatility of our synthetic approach for preparing defect-rich Pd-based alloys.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out to analyze the surface chemical
composition and electronic states of the catalysts. The XPS survey spectra of the PdCuCo samples
confirm the simultaneous presence of Pd, Cu, and Co elements (Supplementary Fig. S7a). In the
Pd 3d XPS spectra (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. S7b), two main peaks at 339.7 eV and 334.4
eV are ascribed to metallic Pd0, alongside two lower-intensity peaks at 340.6 eV and 335.2 eV are
attributed to oxidized Pd2+ species.26 Notably, the Pd 3d binding energies in PdCuCo-0.9 and PdCu
exhibit negative shifts relative to pure Pd, indicating charge transfer from Cu/Co to Pd atoms,
mediated by their strong p-d orbital hybrid interaction.27 The Cu 2p XPS spectra (Fig. 3b and
Supplementary Fig. S7c) reveal two sharp peaks at 930.9 eV and 950.7 eV, confirming the
presence of metallic Cu0.28 Furthermore, the valence band spectra (VBS) in Fig. 3c demonstrate a
pronounced downshift in the d-band center for PdCuCo-0.9 (-2.85 eV) compared to PdCu (-2.70
eV) and Pd (-2.57 eV), signifying a modulated electronic state that weakens the adsorption of
carbonyl (CO*) intermediates on PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene.29, 30 These XPS and VBS analyses
corroborate the metallic nature of constituent elements and highlight the modulated electronic
environment around Pd atoms in PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene. Optimizing the electronic structure
near Pd can facilitate the binding of reaction intermediates at the Pd site, accelerating the
conversion of CO* intermediates and promoting the incomplete oxidation of EG to GA.29

The coordination environment and local electronic structure of each element in PdCuCo-0.9
trimetallene were further investigated using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). The
normalized X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra (Fig. 3d-3e and Supplementary
Fig. S8) at Pd, Cu, and Co K-edges exhibit absorption edges nearly identical to pure metal foils,
confirming the metallic states of all constituent elements and corroborating XPS results. Fourier
transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) analysis at Pd K-edge reveals a
dominant peak at 2.68 Å for PdCuCo-0.9 (Fig. 3f), corresponding to the Pd-Pd/Cu/Co coordination.
Notably, the Pd-Pd/Cu/Co peak exhibits a ~0.04 Å negative shift relative to the Pd foil and
monometallic Pd sample, which is considered to be due to lattice compression induced by smaller
Cu/Co atoms.31 Spectral fitting indicates a reduced coordination number for Pd-Pd/Cu/Co bond in
PdCuCo-0.9 (10.8±1.2 vs. 12 for Pd foil), confirming abundant structural defects and dangling
bonds at the trimetallene surface (Fig. S9, and Supplementary Table S2).32 Furthermore, the
shortened bond length of Pd-Pd/Cu/Co (2.61 Å vs. 2.74 Å for Pd foil) quantitatively demonstrates
compressive strain in PdCuCo-0.9, being consistent with the XRD and TEM observations
(Supplementary Table S2). Wavelet transform analysis further verifies the modified coordination
environment of PdCuCo-0.9 through a distinct pattern from PdO and narrower intensity
distributions in the K range than those of Pd foils.33 Complementary Cu and Co K-edge analyses
(Fig. 3g-3h and Supplementary Fig. S10-S12) yield consistent conclusions, collectively
demonstrating successful synthesis of strained PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene with modulated local
electronic structure of Pd active sites.

Electrocatalytic EGOR and ORR performances of PdCuCo trimetallenes
The EGOR performance of the as-prepared catalysts was primarily evaluated in 1.0 M
KOH+1.0 M EG solution. As displayed in the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves
(Supplementary Fig. S13a), the recorded onset potential for EGOR is significantly lower than that
of the OER on the same electrode. In particular, only an EGOR potential of 0.92 V (vs. RHE) was
required for PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene to deliver a current density of 100 mA cm-2 (Supplementary
Fig. S13b), which is about 1030 mV lower than that of OER. These results confirm the
thermodynamically favorable nature of EGOR over OER, highlighting its realistic feasibility for
substituting OER in D-ZEAB. Mass-normalized cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves display distinct
anodic peaks during the forward/reverse scanning of all catalysts (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig.
S14), which correspond to the ethylene glycol oxidation. Notably, the mass activity (MA) of
PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene attained 11.9 A mg -1(Fig. 4b), which is 1.6, 3.1, and 4.0 times higher
Pd
than that of PdCu, Pd, and Pd black, respectively. The smallest Tafel slope of PdCuCo-0.9
trimetallene (127.8 mV dec-1) further reflected its rapid charge transfer kinetics during EGOR
(Supplementary Fig. S15). The electrocatalytically active surface areas (ECSA) were determined
to be 80.7, 63.0, 41.3, and 55.1 m2 g -1 for PdCuCo-0.9, PdCu, Pd, and Pd black, respectively by
Pd
the CV method (Supplementary Fig. S16 and S17). The larger ECSA value of PdCuCo-0.9 is
attributed to its thin 2D sheet-like morphology and defect-rich structure, which maximizes active
site density and Pd utilization. Moreover, specific activity (SA) calculations normalized to ECSA
further confirm the notable EGOR performance of PdCuCo-0.9 (9.7 mA cm-2), exceeding all
control catalysts (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. S18). The stability of catalysts toward EGOR
was evaluated through CV tests. After 500 CV cycles, the EGOR mass activity of PdCuCo-0.9
was still up to 10.5 A mg -1, with a decay rate of only 12%, outperforming commercial Pd black
Pd
and underscoring its notable electrochemical stability (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. S19). The
notable EGOR performance of PdCuCo-0.9 can be attributed to the highly exposed active Pd sites
enabled by its metallene structure, as well as the tuned electronic structure originating from the
lattice defects and alloying effect among the multiple elements.

Next, the EGOR performance of PdCuCo trimetallenes was further investigated using the
PET hydrolysate solution as electrolyte (Supplementary Fig. S20). Fig. 4e shows the CV curves
of the catalysts in alkaline PET hydrolysate solution, which exhibit EGOR profiles similar to those
observed in 1.0 M KOH+1.0 M EG electrolyte. Notably, PdCuCo-0.9 achieves a high peak mass
activity of 16.6 A mg -1, surpassing the mass activities of Pd black, Pd, PdCu, PdCuCo-0.3, and
Pd
PdCuCo-1.7, and is comparable to the advanced EGOR catalysts reported in references
(Supplementary Fig. S21 and Table S3). Furthermore, among all as-synthesized catalysts and
commercial Pd black, PdCuCo-0.9 demonstrated the high geometric activity (Supplementary Fig.
S22). After a 5 h chronoamperometric (in-t) test at 0.77 V (vs. RHE), PdCuCo-0.9 retained 42%
of its initial current density, exceeding the performance of control samples in this work, confirming
the notable stability (Fig. 4f). EGOR products were further quantified by 1H nuclear magnetic
resonance (NMR) spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. S23 and S24). GA, identified by its distinct
peak at 3.8 ppm in the NMR spectrum, is the primary EGOR product of PdCuCo-0.9, with no
detectable formic acid (FA) byproduct, suggesting its high GA selectivity. Furthermore, PdCuCo-
0.9 achieves a GA Faradaic efficiency (FE ) exceeding 90% over a wide potential range from
GA
0.7 to 1.0 V (vs. RHE), reflecting its high selectivity for GA synthesis via the electroreforming of
PET wastes (Fig. 4g). Remarkably, the maximum FE and GA yield rate of PdCuCo-0.9 reach
GA
up to 94.8% and 0.32 mmol cm-2 h-1 at 0.85 V (vs. RHE), respectively, rivaling recently reported
advanced EGOR catalysts (Supplementary Table S4).

The ORR performance of PdCuCo trimetallenes was then assessed in O -saturated 0.1 M
2
KOH. As presented in Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. S25a, PdCuCo-0.9 exhibits a half-wave
potential (E ) of 0.90 V vs. RHE, surpassing the E values of PdCu, Pd, and commercial Pt/C
1/2 1/2
by 40, 60, and 50 mV, respectively, signifying notable ORR activity. Among all tested catalysts,
including Pt/C, PdCuCo-0.9 held the smallest Tafel slope (71.0 mV dec-1), reflecting the favorable
ORR kinetics (Supplementary Fig. S25b).34, 35 The average electron transfer number close to 4 and
low H O yield (< 6%) for PdCuCo-0.9 over 0.2 to 0.9 V (vs. RHE) confirm a dominant 4e- transfer
2 2
ORR pathway (Supplementary Fig. S25c). Durability testing via chronoamperometry displayed
93.6% current retention after 11 h, while 2000 CV cycles caused negligible E
1/2
loss, demonstrating
respectable ORR stability and performance reproducibility (Fig. 4i; Supplementary Fig. S25d).
The enhanced ORR activity of PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene arises from its defect-rich structure, which
maximizes active Pd site density and utilization, while Cu/Co incorporation facilitates O
2
adsorption/dissociation into *O intermediates for efficient 4e- pathways.36

Reaction mechanism investigations and theoretical calculations.
The adsorption behavior of EG molecules on the catalyst surface was initially investigated
using the open-circuit potential (OCP) measurements (Supplementary Fig. S26). When switching
to PET electrolyte, the OCP of PdCuCo-0.9 decreased by 0.84 V, exceeding the OCP reductions
of PdCu (0.77 V) and Pd (0.65 V), reflecting its notable affinity for EG. CO stripping experiments
reveal that the oxidation potential of the CO* intermediate on PdCuCo-0.9 is 0.77 V
(Supplementary Fig. S27), which is 20 mV and 40 mV lower than those on PdCu and Pd,
respectively, indicating the weaker CO* adsorption on PdCuCo-0.9.29 This facilitates the rapid
desorption and subsequent conversion of carbonyl (CO*) intermediates during the EGOR process,
thereby maintaining a highly active catalyst surface and promoting high selectivity toward GA.37
In situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis demonstrated that PdCuCo-0.9
exhibits a lower charge transfer resistance and phase angle compared to both PdCu and Pd black,
suggesting its faster reaction kinetics (Fig. 5a, 5b; Supplementary Fig. S28 and Table S5).38 This
enhanced kinetic behavior can be attributed to the synergistic effects of abundant lattice defects,
metallene architecture, and multi-element alloying, which collectively accelerate the EGOR
kinetics of PdCuCo-0.9.

To gain insight into the reaction mechanism of the EGOR on PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene, in
situ electrochemical attenuated total reflection surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy
(ATR-SEIRAS) and Raman spectroscopy measurements were performed to identify key reaction
intermediates. As displayed in the in situ ATR-SEIRAS spectra (Fig. 5c), the characteristic peaks
located at 1043 cm-1 and 1086 cm-1 are attributed to the stretching vibration of the GA species.39
The peaks at 1258 cm-1, 1362 cm-1 and 1336 cm-1 belong to the symmetric and antisymmetric
stretching vibrations of COO- in GA.40 The intensity of above characteristic peaks increases with
the increase of potential, indicating the continuous generation of GA during EG oxidation. Notably,
the GA-associated peak (1043 cm-1, 1086 cm-1 and 1258 cm-1) exhibits markedly higher intensity
on PdCuCo-0.9 compared to those of pure Pd and PdCu, confirming its notable selectivity for GA
production (Fig. 5d and Supplementary Fig. S29). Additionally, there is a distinct peak at 1646 cm-
1 corresponding to the CH OHCO* intermediate, which is a key intermediate in the EGOR process
2
of the C pathway.41 Meanwhile, the signal of FA was hardly observed at 1376 cm-1.42 Furthermore,
2
no clear hydroxyl radicals (•OH) signal was detected by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)
at 1.0 V (vs. RHE) for PdCuCo-0.9, demonstrating that •OH do not play a major role in mediating
the EGOR on this catalyst (Fig. 5e). Fig. 5f illustrates the potential-dependent in situ Raman
spectra of PdCuCo-0.9 recorded in 1.0 M KOH+1.0 M EG. As the applied potentials was increased
from 0.5 to 1.1 V (vs. RHE), distinct Raman peaks was emerged at 478 cm-1, 557 cm-1, and 652
cm-1. These signal are characteristic of the Pd-O stretching vibration associated with Pd-OH and
ad
Pd-O (denoted as Pd-O(H) ) species generated during glycolate formation.43 Notably, LSV
ad ad
measurement revealed no significant evidence of palladium oxide formation within the potential
range of 0.5 V-1.1 V (Supplementary Fig. S13), suggesting that the observed Pd-O(H) species
ad
formed in situ on PdCuCo-0.9 differ from typical PdO oxide. Under identical conditions, these
x
Pd-O(H) -related Raman signals exhibited significantly reduced intensity on the PdCu and were
ad
barely detectable on the pure Pd sample (Fig. 5g and Supplementary Fig. S30). Additional peaks
at 1355 cm-1, 1427 cm-1, and 1579 cm-1 are attributed to COO- symmetric and asymmetric
stretching vibration of GA.44 Collectively, the aforementioned in situ characterizations and EPR
analysis confirm that the in situ formed Pd-O(H) species on the PdCuCo catalyst surface strongly
ad
suppressed the cleavage of the C-C bond in intermediates, thereby contributing to a rapid reaction
pathway from EG to glycolate (Fig. 5h and Supplementary Fig. S31).

To explore the origins of the notable EGOR performance of PdCuCo-0.9, density functional
theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to investigate differences in electronic structures and
reaction energetics among various electrocatalysts. For all the catalyst surfaces, the most preferred
adsorption sites are near the Pd-top site, supporting that Pd is the main active site (Supplementary
Fig. S32-S34). The surface electronic distribution of PdCu and PdCuCo-0.9 was analyzed via
bonding and anti-bonding orbital distributions near the Fermi level (E) (Fig. 6a and 6b). By
f
introducing Co atoms, the orbital coupling at the Pd site in PdCuCo-0.9 is slightly weakened due
to electron modulation, indicating an enhanced electron richness of Pd. Meanwhile, the surface Co
sites exhibit significant orbital coupling, which is conducive to electron transfer/exchange and
thereby enhances the electroactivity of PdCuCo-0.9. Fig. 6c displays the bond length contraction
trends of different catalysts: Pd > PdCu > PdCuCo-0.9, indicating that the introduction of Cu/Co
induces a stronger lattice compression strain, which is consistent with the HAADF-STEM results.
Projected partial density of states (PDOS) comparisons between PdCu and PdCuCo-0.9 show Cu-
3d orbitals with sharp peaks at lower energies than E (Fig. 6d and 6e), positioning Cu as an
f
electron reservoir to modulate adjacent Pd sites. Conversely, the Pd-4d orbitals are located near
the E as the main active sites for EGOR. With the introduction of Co sites, the Pd-4d orbitals
f
slightly downshifted and became more concentrated, which weakened the adsorption strengths of
key intermediates and accelerated the subsequent conversion processes. Notably, the Co-3d
orbitals display a distinct E-adjacent peak, which contributes to the surface electron transfer
f
during EGOR. The d-band center shifts further confirm these trends, with both overall structures
and Pd sites exhibiting downward shifts (Fig. 6f). Mulliken charge analysis reveals reduced Pd
surface charge due to electron donation from positively charged Co sites, while electron-rich Cu
sites exhibit the most negative charges (Fig. 6g), optimizing the surface electroactivity. These
results support the XPS and VBS characterizations that more electrons are transferred from Cu/Co
to the Pd sites, which alleviates the adsorptions of key intermediates to improve the selectivity of
GA production.

The site-dependent PDOS of Pd sites in PdCuCo-0.9 reveals electronic structure changes
near the E (Fig. 6h). Compared to the pristine Pd surface, Pd-4d orbitals in PdCuCo-0.9 localize
f
toward the surface, promoting electron transfer. Meanwhile, the electron density near the E is
f
gradually decreases, which leads to weakened intermediate binding strengths during EGOR. In
contrast, Cu-3d orbitals display increased spatial confinement while maintaining similar d-band
center positions (Fig. 6i), revealing Cu's role as an electron reservoir to modulate Pd electronic
states. Adsorption energy analyses demonstrate distinct trends: PdCuCo-0.9 exhibits the strongest
EG* affinity, whereas CH OHCO* binding energies increase progressively from PdCuCo-0.9 to
2
Pd (Fig. 6j). This trend indicates that the notable performance of PdCuCo-0.9 in converting EG to
GA stems from the activation of reactants and the rapid conversion of intermediates. The analysis
of reaction free energy further revealed that the rate-determining steps (RDS) of Pd and PdCuCo-
0.9/PdCu were the formation processes of CH OHCH O* and CH OHCO*, respectively.
2 2 2
Compared with Pd (0.81 eV) and PdCu (0.44 eV), the RDS barrier of PdCuCo-0.9 was
significantly reduced to 0.25 eV, thereby achieving efficient EGOR performance (Fig. 6k).

Performance of rechargeable D-ZEAB based on PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene
As a proof-of-concept study, a rechargeable D-ZEAB was assembled using PdCuCo-0.9
trimetallene as a bifunctional catalyst, with EGOR and ORR decoupled on two independent
cathodes (Supplementary Fig. S35). A mixed solution of 1.0 M KOH+1.0 M EG was served as the
charging electrolyte. For comparison, single-cathode zinc-ethylene glycol-air battery (S-ZEAB)
and dual-cathode zinc-air battery (D-ZAB) were also assembled using PdCuCo-0.9 catalysts
(Supplementary Fig. S36). As shown in Fig. 7a, the discharging voltage of D-ZEAB was at least
190 mV higher than that of S-ZEAB across 5~50 mA cm-2, demonstrating the decoupled cathodes
eliminate the adverse effect of concomitant EG in electrolyte during ORR and maintain optimal
reaction thermodynamics. At 5 mAh cm-2, D-ZEAB exhibits a significantly lower charging voltage
(1.31 V vs. 2.07 V for D-ZAB), highlighting ~32% higher charging efficiency via EGOR
substitution for OER (Supplementary Fig. S37a-S37d). Notably, EGOR replacement greatly
enhances the charging/discharging energy conversion efficiency (ECE) from 55.1% (D-ZAB) to
87.0% (D-ZEAB), confirming notable energy savings. Unlike D-ZAB, D-ZEAB prioritizes liquid
C chemicals during charging (Supplementary Fig. S37e), eliminating the formation of O and the
2 2
catalyst loss resulting from the bubble impulse, thereby extending the service life of battery. After
48 h continuous cycling, the FE remains >94.0% (Supplementary Fig. S37f and S37g),
GA
validating high and stable GA production efficiency in the PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB system.
To expand its practical applications, the performance of D-ZEAB using PET hydrolysate
solution as the charging electrolyte was investigated. Both the PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB and
ZAB delivered an energy density of approximately 868 Wh kg-1, which is 13.8% higher than that
of the Pt/C + Pd black reference system (763 Wh kg-1) and comparable to the recently reported
advanced ZABs, highlighting the notable energy storage performance of this catalyst (Fig. 7b and
Supplementary Table S6). Fig. 7c and Supplementary Fig. S38 show the galvanostatic
charging/discharging cycling curves of batteries at the areal discharging capacity of 5 mAh cm-2
per cycle. The PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB exhibits a narrow charging/discharging voltage gap
(∆E) of 50 mV and a high ECE of 95.7%, outperforming Pt/C+Pd black-based D-ZEAB
(Supplementary Fig. S39). Compared with the reported conventional ZABs, the PdCuCo-0.9-
based D-ZEAB is also competitive (Supplementary Table S7). In particular, only a slight decrease
of ∆E and ECE values were observed for PdCuCo-0.9 based D-ZEAB after continuous
discharging/charging for 848 cycles (a total of 1696 h), demonstrating an notable cycling stability.
Even at 10 mAh cm-2, the PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB still demonstrates an ECE of no less than
66.0% and maintains stable cycling for 615 h (Supplementary Fig. S40). Besides, the thin 2D
sheet-like morphology and defect-rich structure of PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene after long-term
cycling tests are well preserved, verifying the structural stability (Supplementary Fig. S41 and
S42). Notably, unlike the partial oxidation of the catalyst on charging the cathode, the metallic
character and single-phase fcc structure of PdCuCo-0.9 on discharging the cathode are maintained
after long-term cycling tests (Supplementary Fig. S43 and S44). This significant difference
highlights the advantages of the spatially decoupled cathode structure of D-ZEAB in terms of
avoiding oxidation and deactivation of the ORR catalyst.

Finally, the EGOR products in the charging electrolyte of the PdCuCo-0.9 based D-ZEAB
were identified by 1H NMR spectroscopy under different cycling periods. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. S45 and S46, GA was identified as the main product during the charging
process, with trace amounts of FA by-products. The FE
GA
on the charging cathode remained above
93.0% at the areal discharging capacities of 5 and 10 mAh cm-2 per cycle, confirming the high
selectivity of GA production via PET electroreforming during the charging process of PdCuCo-
0.9 based D-ZEAB (Fig. 7d). To achieve effective resource recovery and recycling, we further
separated and purified the high-value products from the charging electrolyte after cycling tests.
Ultimately, 40.36 g TPA and 8.51 g GA were obtained from the electroreforming of 50 g PET
plastic waste (Fig. 7e and Supplementary Fig. S47), achieving a total mass yield of 97.7% for
products. The preliminary techno-economic analysis demonstrated that although the initial input
cost for the D-ZEAB exceeds that of a conventional ZAB by $466.7 per ton of processed PET, it
generates a substantially higher total output value ($2,346.3 versus $82.5). This yields a net profit
of $276.5 per ton of processed PET, confirming the D-ZEAB's economic viability (Supplementary
Tables S8-S11 and Fig. S48-S49). Notably, compared to existing aqueous zinc-based batteries
(Supplementary Table S12), the D-ZEAB proposed in this work exhibits comprehensive
superiority over critical performance metrics, including cycle life, energy conversion efficiency,
discharging capacity, and functionality, demonstrating promising application prospects.

### Reviewer 1

The authors introduce the EGOR reaction to address the slow kinetics of the OER in conventional zinc–air batteries, and
they further aim to achieve upcycling by employing PET plastic hydrolysate. As a result, they propose an environmentally
friendly battery system with high charging efficiency that utilizes waste plastics. To further validate the creativity and practical
relevance of this work, I suggest addressing the following points:
1. The EGOR cathode and ORR cathode are separated by a Nafion 117 membrane. Does this membrane sufficiently
prevent crossover between the two electrolytes? If available, please provide data or discussion on crossover performance.
2. While the concept of recycling PET to produce GA in this system is highly noteworthy, the catalyst employed contains
precious metal Pd, which could be at odds with the claimed economic benefits of recycling. Please discuss the recyclability
or recovery strategy for Pd and provide a perspective on the economic feasibility of this aspect. Additionally, consider
commenting on possible screening or substitution of other non-precious metal elements.
3. As highlighted, one of the main discussion points of this paper is the recycling profits. Much of the techno-economic
analysis is contained on the supplementary information. Consider including more of this discussion in the main text if
necessary.
4. The supporting information suggests that zinc oxide reacts with ethylene glycol to facilitate zinc electrodeposition. Does
this system avoid the passivation issues typically associated with ZnO formation in conventional ZABs? Please provide your
thoughts on this point.
5. How were the experimental setups for S-ZEAB and D-ZEAB configured? Please describe these in more detail (photos or
figures).
6. For practical applicability, please discuss the potential for scaling up to larger electrode areas and cell formats.
7. While the electrochemical performance profiles of the PET hydrolysate and pure EG electrolyte appear similar, what are
the expected impacts of by-products and impurities on the system if PET hydrolysate is used in a large-scale, high-capacity,
long-term setup?
8. In the full-cell experiments, how was the operating temperature controlled? Additionally, what criteria were used to
manage or replace the zinc anode?

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Li et al. presents a dual-cathode zinc-ethylene glycol/air battery (D-ZEAB) that spatially decouples ORR
and the ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR) onto separate cathodes, enabling concurrent electricity generation and
electroreforming of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic waste into high-value C2 chemicals. In general, the authors did
a lot of work for this paper, while the novelty is not high to me. After struggling, I decided to reject it. Detailed review
comments are as follows:
1. From plastic waste into high-value C2 chemicals is a great way in green chemistry, and here is the EGOR for converting
EG to GA during charging for ZAB. However, the end-users only care about the ZAB price and energy density, and the GA
recovery is meaningless to them, plus the complex purify step to get pure GA. Therefore, the economic analysis does not
make sense to me.
2. Since it is not practical for users to refresh the EG and electrolytes, this design changes the rechargeable ZAB to one-time
use with the continuous consumption of EG. Also, the two-cathode design will increase the capital cost.
3. The PdCuCo catalyst exhibits remarkable catalytic performance for ethylene glycol. However, considering that the authors
compared the catalysts in the current reported literature based on the current activity current of Pd, it is necessary to
determine whether this catalyst still has an advantage when compared based on the activity per unit area. And from the CV
curve in Figure 4, the oxidation overpotential of ethylene glycol is much higher than its theoretical potential. Even when the
current increases, it approaches the reaction potential of OER. Is the advantage of this system over the OER reaction
accurate?
4. From Supplementary Fig. S18, it seems there is no obvious current difference between the Pd and PdCuCo-0.9 catalysts
in terms of ECSA-normalized CV curves, indicating the enhanced activity of PdCuCo-0.9 catalyst can only be attributed to
the increased ECSA instead of forming higher active sites, which conflicts with the finding and conclusion in this work.
This is critical.
5. In this work, 0.1 M, 1 M, 4 M and 6 M KOH electrolytes were used for investigating the activity of catalysts and
performance of battery, making me confused. Why was there not constant electrolyte concentration used?
6. For the battery test, “(1) a porous zinc plate (99.99% purity) as anode; (2) a charging cathode with 1.0 M KOH+1.0 M EG or
PET hydrolysate solution as the electrolyte; (3) a discharging cathode containing 6.0 M KOH+0.2 M Zn(OAc)2 electrolyte;
and (4) a Nafion 117 membrane separating the charging/discharging electrolytes.” 1 M and 6 M KOH electrolytes were used
in the two cathodes, respectively. How do you balance the hydroxides produced and consumed from two cathodes? We
know that Nafion membrane can block the hydroxide transfer, while it can allow the potassium transfer. Also, the refreshing
electrolyte every 24 h is not practical. This part needs to be paid more attention.
7. As can be seen in Figure 7e, the overpotential during the charging process is extremely high, especially under high
current conditions. A comparison with ZABs should be provided, and it should be considered whether the loss of charging
current in this system is meaningful without a significant reduction in charging voltage.
8. The depiction of the reaction process and the device structure in Figure 1a is confusing and unclear. In Figure 1b, the
oxidation of ethylene glycol is labeled as the reaction of ethanol oxidizing to acetic acid. This may mislead the readers.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript addresses the use of Pd-based catalysts in zinc–air batteries. The authors propose an electrocatalyst for
ethylene glycol/PET electrooxidation and oxygen reduction reactions. The innovative aspect of this work lies in the use of a
dual-cathode battery, in which the charging reaction at one of the cathodes occurs via the oxidation of ethylene glycol
derived from plastic waste. This approach makes the process both environmentally and commercially attractive, in addition
to lowering energy costs, since the oxygen evolution reaction typically occurs at high overpotentials.
The manuscript is well-structured in both writing and organization of results, following a logical sequence that allows for
smooth reading and easy comprehension.The references used by the authors are current and consistent with the theme
proposed in the manuscript.
Scientifically, the electrocatalyst was characterized using key surface techniques (XRD, EDS, XPS, SVB, and XAS), while
its morphology and microstructure were examined using TEM and HAADF-STEM. The discussion of these characterization
results effectively clarifies the physical and chemical composition of the synthesized materials and how each element
contributes to the relationship between their chemical, electronic, and structural states in the studied reactions.
Regarding the analysis of reaction intermediates, the authors employed NMR and FTIR to monitor the formation of the major
species generated during the application of potential. Theoretical studies were conducted to provide a more in-depth
discussion of the energetic contributions of Cu and Co incorporated into Pd, which, to some extent, shed light on the
adsorption processes of ethylene glycol (EG) and its reaction intermediates.
However, I have some comments on the manuscript that require minor revisions so that the final work meets the necessary
standards for approval and publication in Nature Communications.
Below are my comments:
1.In my opinion, the authors should address the main motivation for studying the synthesized electrocatalyst in the
introduction. Numerous studies in the literature focus on the electrooxidation of alcohols, particularly ethylene glycol, which
is a widely studied organic molecule for various applications. The rationale for selecting a PdCuCo-based catalyst remains
unclear. A discussion of the main electrocatalysts used for this purpose could help clarify how this work advances the
frontiers of knowledge in this area.
2. Another point that caught my attention concerns the use of such a high noble-metal loading, given that the current trend is
to minimize or even eliminate the use of noble metals by replacing them with more abundant and less expensive
alternatives. Palladium is among the most expensive noble metals. Considering the practical application of the proposed
battery, would the high Pd content be commercially viable? I invite the authors to comment on this aspect.
Also, the authors compare the performance of the synthesized material with others in the literature (Figure 4f). While it is
important to highlight the performance of the material used compared to others, these comparisons often do not reflect
reality. I say this because the amount of metal (Pd) used by the authors is significant, even with normalization. Other studies
may use non-noble metals or even a reduced amount of Pd, which results in lower current densities.
3. Regarding the experiments presented, I have the following considerations:
3.1. Indicate in the figures 4(a,e) which voltammetric cycles are shown (first, second, third, etc.).
3.2. Regarding the in situ FTIR experiments, the authors used ATR-SEIRAS to analyze the intermediates formed during the
oxidation of EG. I recommend more details about the experimental procedure for obtaining the catalyst layer on the silicon
prism coated with the metal film.
I have some specific observations concerning the FTIR discussion.
The oxidation of organics on Pd is well discussed in the literature, and it is known that electrocatalytic activity depends on
the supporting electrolyte and pH. In alkaline media, bands at 1575, 14109, 1324, and 1075 cm⁻¹ can be attributed to the
formation of intermediates such as glyoxal and glycolate, which can subsequently be oxidized to glyoxylate, with the
appearance of a band at 1363 cm⁻¹ at higher potentials.
As the potential increases, a band may also appear at 1310 cm⁻¹, indicating the formation of oxalate. At high potentials,
formate can be produced, with characteristic bands at 2820, 2740, 1386, and 1353 cm⁻¹.
The carbonate ion band (1370 cm⁻¹) is typically not visible in the spectra due to overlap with the band at 1409 cm⁻¹,
although its presence can be inferred from the pronounced broadening of the latter.
It is also worth noting that glyoxal and glycolate are generally the primary products of EG electrooxidation at lower potentials.
Then, taking into accoun the above considerations about this system, the authors state that the reaction mechanism involves
the formation of glycolaldehyde; however, in alkaline media, this species is rarely identified because it tends to undergo self-
polymerization.
Regarding CO, on Pd surfaces, its formation is not easily detected in either acidic or
alkaline media. This suggests that the reaction pathway may proceed directly without CO
as an intermediate, or that CO, being only weakly adsorbed on Pd, is rapidly oxidized.
Therefore, given that the manuscript asserts the formation of CO as part of the mechanism, I encourage the authors to
reconsider whether the proposed pathway is in fact the most plausible one.

## Paper

## Abstract

Conventional rechargeable zinc-air batteries (ZABs) face two critical challenges: (1) slow
kinetics of the oxygen reduction (ORR) and oxygen evolution (OER) reactions; and (2) the
thermodynamic incompatibility of OER and ORR occurring concurrently on a single air cathode.
To address these limitations, we propose in this study a dual-cathode zinc-ethylene glycol/air
battery (D-ZEAB) that spatially decouples ORR and the ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR)
onto separate cathodes, enabling concurrent electricity generation and electroreforming of
polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic waste into high-value C chemicals. Furthermore, we
develop a bifunctional catalyst composed of defect- rich subnanometer-thick PdCuCo trimetallenes
to enhance both EGOR and ORR kinetics. Benefiting from the decoupled cathode configuration
and the bifunctional PdCuCo catalyst, the D-ZEAB demonstrates an energy conversion efficiency
of 91.7%, a long cycle life of 1696 h, and a Faradaic efficiency of >93% for GA production. This
work not only presents a promising strategy for advancing the zinc-air battery technology but also
offers a sustainable route for simultaneous energy storage and plastic waste upcycling.

## Introduction

Energy shortage and environmental pollution remain persistent global challenges, driving
the development of sustainable energy storage systems such as metal-air batteries, metal-ion
batteries, metal-sulfur batteries, and fuel cells.1, 2, 3, 4 Among them, rechargeable zinc-air batteries
(ZABs) utilizing atmospheric oxygen as the cathode active substance are widely considered
promising energy storage and conversion devices due to their high theoretical energy density (1350
Wh kg-1), cost-effectiveness, and environmental benignity.5, 6 A typical ZAB consists of a zinc
anode, an aqueous electrolyte, and a bifunctional air cathode that facilitates oxygen reduction
(ORR) during discharge and oxygen evolution (OER) during charge.7, 8 However, the
commercialization of ZABs remains hindered by several limitations: (1) the absence of cost-
effective bifunctional electrocatalysts that can enhance the sluggish ORR and OER kinetics leads
to low per-cycle capacity, large charging/discharging voltage gaps (∆E), and reduced energy
conversion efficiency; (2) the single-cathode configuration requires both ORR and OER to occur
on the same electrode, which, due to their opposing thermodynamic requirements, accelerates
catalyst oxidation and deactivation, thus reducing the discharging capacity and cycle life of the
batteries; (3) the charging process produces low-value oxygen, which undermines the economic
viability of ZABs. Thus, strategies to improve the energy efficiency, economic efficiency, and
operational stability of ZABs are urgently needed.

Recently, a class of zinc-X/air hybrid batteries (ZXAHBs, X = KI, alcohol, or urea) has been
proposed, wherein the kinetically sluggish OER is replaced with thermodynamically favorable
oxidation reactions (XOR) involving readily oxidizable substances, such as KI, alcohol, and urea.9,
10, 11, 12 These hybrid batteries demonstrate a significant improvement in energy conversion
efficiency by lowering the required charging voltages. However, despite their enhanced charging
performance, challenges persist, including: the unresolved thermodynamic mismatch between
ORR and XOR on a single air cathode; the absence of highly active and selective bifunctional
catalysts for both ORR and XOR; the low economic value of products generated during the battery
charging process (e.g., N from urea oxidation, and CO from most alcohol oxidations);11, 13, 14 and
2 2
the potential battery safety hazards arising from the introduction of flammable organic compounds
(e.g., methanol, ethanol) into the electrolyte. As a result, most reported ZXAHBs demonstrate only
modest performance, with areal discharging capacities ≤ 2 mAh cm-2 per cycle and cycle lifetimes
≤ 400 h.15, 16 To meet the demands of large-scale commercialization, zinc-air and hybrid batteries
must overcome these kinetic and thermodynamic limitations, achieving high areal capacity, energy
conversion efficiency, product selectivity, and long -term stability.

In this work, we introduce a dual-cathode zinc-ethylene glycol/air battery (D-ZEAB) that
spatially decouples the ORR and ethylene glycol oxidation reaction (EGOR) onto separate
cathodes. This design enables simultaneous electricity generation and electroreforming of PET
plastic waste into high-value C chemicals. By isolating the two reactions, the D-ZEAB optimizes
2
the thermodynamic conditions for EGOR (charging) and ORR (discharging), while preventing the
oxidation of ORR catalyst. Thereby, the discharging capacity and cycle life are both enhanced.
Moreover, replacing OER with the thermodynamically favorable EGOR significantly reduces
charging voltages and improves energy conversion efficiency. From a kinetic perspective, efficient
catalysts with low overpotentials for ethylene glycol-to-glycolic acid oxidation and the ORR are
required to enable high-performance operation of D-ZEAB. While Pd exhibits high activity for
both EGOR and ORR, its practical application is hindered by challenges in atomic utilization, mass
activity, and stability.17, 18 Integrating alloying and structure engineering to design Pd-based
trimetallene aims to retain high atomic utilization via quantum size effect and synergistically
optimize EGOR/ORR performance through ternary component interactions and tailored
architectures. Therefore, defect-rich PdCuCo trimetallene was further engineered as dual-cathode
catalyst to accelerate EGOR/ORR kinetics. Leveraging synergistic structural (e.g., lattice defects,
compressive strain, and metallene architecture) and alloying effects, the optimized PdCuCo-0.9
achieves high electrocatalytic performance: an EGOR mass activity of 16.6 A mg -1, an ORR half-
Pd
wave potential of 0.90 V (vs. RHE), and notable durability. In situ experiments and density
functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the synergistic structural and alloying effects
modulate the electronic structure of Pd sites on PdCuCo. This modulation weakens the adsorption
of the carbonyl (*CO) intermediate intermediate and accelerates the in situ formation of Pd-O(H)
ad
species, thereby facilitating the selective oxidation from ethylene glycol to glycolic acid (GA).
As a result of the decoupled cathode configuration and the notable bifunctional catalytic activity,
the
PdCuCo-based D-ZEAB achieves an energy density of 868 Wh kg-1, a discharging capacity of 10
mAh per cycle, and a long cycle life of 1696 h, with a Faradaic efficiency exceeding 93% for GA
production. Notably, the battery retains a high energy conversion efficiency of 91.7% even after
1696 h of continuous cycling.

## Results

Design and working principle of rechargeable D-ZEAB
Fig. 1a schematically illustrates the configuration and working mechanism of the
rechargeable D-ZEAB. The battery features four key components: (1) a porous zinc anode; (2) a
charging cathode utilizing PET hydrolysate solution as electrolyte; (3) a discharging cathode with
6.0 M KOH+0.2 M Zn(OAc) mixed electrolyte; and (4) a membrane separating the two
2
electrolytes. This spatially decoupled cathode configuration enables the ORR and EGOR to
proceed independently under their respective optimal thermodynamic conditions without
interfering with each other. During operation, the system automatically switches between two
modes: charging (EGOR at one cathode to produce high-value GA) and discharging (ORR at the
other cathode). The detailed reaction pathways and the thermodynamic calculations provided in
Supplementary Eqs. S1-S9. Unlike conventional ZABs that are limited by the sluggish OER, the
charging process of D-ZEAB is significantly optimized by the low oxidation potential (~0.2 V vs.
SHE) and fast kinetics of EGOR.19 Theoretical calculations indicate that the D-ZEAB achieves an
low charging voltage of ~0.623 V (Supplementary Eqs. S9), representing a reduction of at least
1.030 V compared to typical ZABs (Fig. 1b). Additionally, the decoupled cathode design prevents
the oxidation-induced deactivation of ORR catalyst even at high charging voltages, dramatically
enhancing the cycle stability. Notably, the system also offers compelling sustainability advantages:
ethylene glycol (key EGOR reactant) can be abundantly sourced from PET waste hydrolysis,
creating a circular economy.20, 21 Beyond electricity generation during the discharging process, the
D-ZEAB simultaneously produces valuable GA through electroreforming of PET plastic waste.
As shown in Fig. 1c, this integrated approach presents a more cost-effective, energy-efficient, and
environmentally benign alternative to conventional GA production methods, offering significant
potential for addressing global plastic pollution while advancing energy storage technology.

Synthesis and characterization of PdCuCo trimetallenes
To achieve high-efficiency operation of the D-ZEAB, we developed defect-rich PdCuCo
trimetallenes as advanced bifunctional catalysts for simultaneous EGOR and ORR enhancement
(Fig. 2a). The catalysts were synthesized via a one-pot solvothermal method using Pd2+, Cu2+ and
Co2+ precursors with ethylenediamine (EDA) as the reducing agent. The X-ray diffraction (XRD)
analysis of PdCuCo trimetallenes confirms the formation of well-alloyed face-centered cubic (fcc)
phases (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. S1). The diffraction peaks of PdCuCo trimetallenes are
positively shifted compared to pure Pd, indicating the existence of lattice compression due to the
incorporation of Cu/Co with a smaller atomic radius into the Pd lattice. Meanwhile, the broadened
diffraction peaks of PdCuCo trimetallenes suggest reduced crystallite size and the generation of
lattice defects caused by Cu/Co incorporation.22 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and
inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) results verify the
coexistence of Pd, Cu, and Co elements, with a bulk composition of Pd/Cu/Co = 55.0/44.1/0.9 for
PdCuCo-0.9 (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Table S1). High-resolution transmission electron
microscopy (HR-TEM) observations reveal a 2D sheet-like morphology of PdCuCo-0.9 with an
average lateral size of ~20 nm (Fig. 2d and 2e); and atomic force microscopy (AFM) analyses
further verify a metallene structure of PdCuCo -0.9 (~1.0 nm thickness, ~5 atomic layers;
Supplementary Fig. S2). The sub-nanometer metallene architecture is conducive to shortening
diffusion pathways for reactant/intermediate and enhancing mass/charge transfer efficiency during
the electrocatalysis process. The combined structural and compositional features synergistically
contribute to the catalyst's high performance in the D-ZEAB system.23

Atomic-scale lattice configuration of PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene was investigated using
aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM). As denoted
by the blue dashed circles in Fig. 2f and Supplementary Fig. S3, numerous lattice distortions (LDs)
can be observed in PdCuCo-0.9, arising from the atomic size mismatch between Pd, Cu, and Co
constituents. Distinct zigzag atomic steps appear along the curved edges (indicated by red arrows,
Fig. 2g), while the enlarged HAADF-STEM observations further confirm the presence of twin
boundaries (TBs), atomic vacancies (AVs), and stacking faults (SFs) (Fig. 2h-2j). These structural
defects are expected to modulate the surface electronic states and enhance the electrocatalytic
activity.24 The integrated pixel intensities obtained by line-scan along the [111] direction reveal an
average lattice spacing of 2.22 Å for (111) planes (Fig. 2k). This represents an approximately 6.3%
compressive strain in PdCuCo-0.9 relative to the bulk Pd crystal (2.30 Å, JCPDS No. 87-0637),
attributed to atomic size difference and lattice defects.25 EDS mapping further validates
homogenous distribution of Pd, Cu, and Co elements throughout the nanostructure (Fig. 2l and
2m). To assess the impacts of Cu and Co incorporation, control samples including PdCuCo-0.3,
PdCuCo-1.7, PdCu alloy, and monometallic Pd were also synthesized using the same approach.
The representative TEM and EDS elemental mapping images of these control samples reveal
similar lattice defects across these variants (Supplementary Fig. S4-S6), which underscores the
versatility of our synthetic approach for preparing defect-rich Pd-based alloys.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was carried out to analyze the surface chemical
composition and electronic states of the catalysts. The XPS survey spectra of the PdCuCo samples
confirm the simultaneous presence of Pd, Cu, and Co elements (Supplementary Fig. S7a). In the
Pd 3d XPS spectra (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. S7b), two main peaks at 339.7 eV and 334.4
eV are ascribed to metallic Pd0, alongside two lower-intensity peaks at 340.6 eV and 335.2 eV are
attributed to oxidized Pd2+ species.26 Notably, the Pd 3d binding energies in PdCuCo-0.9 and PdCu
exhibit negative shifts relative to pure Pd, indicating charge transfer from Cu/Co to Pd atoms,
mediated by their strong p-d orbital hybrid interaction.27 The Cu 2p XPS spectra (Fig. 3b and
Supplementary Fig. S7c) reveal two sharp peaks at 930.9 eV and 950.7 eV, confirming the
presence of metallic Cu0.28 Furthermore, the valence band spectra (VBS) in Fig. 3c demonstrate a
pronounced downshift in the d-band center for PdCuCo-0.9 (-2.85 eV) compared to PdCu (-2.70
eV) and Pd (-2.57 eV), signifying a modulated electronic state that weakens the adsorption of
carbonyl (CO*) intermediates on PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene.29, 30 These XPS and VBS analyses
corroborate the metallic nature of constituent elements and highlight the modulated electronic
environment around Pd atoms in PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene. Optimizing the electronic structure
near Pd can facilitate the binding of reaction intermediates at the Pd site, accelerating the
conversion of CO* intermediates and promoting the incomplete oxidation of EG to GA.29

The coordination environment and local electronic structure of each element in PdCuCo-0.9
trimetallene were further investigated using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). The
normalized X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra (Fig. 3d-3e and Supplementary
Fig. S8) at Pd, Cu, and Co K-edges exhibit absorption edges nearly identical to pure metal foils,
confirming the metallic states of all constituent elements and corroborating XPS results. Fourier
transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) analysis at Pd K-edge reveals a
dominant peak at 2.68 Å for PdCuCo-0.9 (Fig. 3f), corresponding to the Pd-Pd/Cu/Co coordination.
Notably, the Pd-Pd/Cu/Co peak exhibits a ~0.04 Å negative shift relative to the Pd foil and
monometallic Pd sample, which is considered to be due to lattice compression induced by smaller
Cu/Co atoms.31 Spectral fitting indicates a reduced coordination number for Pd-Pd/Cu/Co bond in
PdCuCo-0.9 (10.8±1.2 vs. 12 for Pd foil), confirming abundant structural defects and dangling
bonds at the trimetallene surface (Fig. S9, and Supplementary Table S2).32 Furthermore, the
shortened bond length of Pd-Pd/Cu/Co (2.61 Å vs. 2.74 Å for Pd foil) quantitatively demonstrates
compressive strain in PdCuCo-0.9, being consistent with the XRD and TEM observations
(Supplementary Table S2). Wavelet transform analysis further verifies the modified coordination
environment of PdCuCo-0.9 through a distinct pattern from PdO and narrower intensity
distributions in the K range than those of Pd foils.33 Complementary Cu and Co K-edge analyses
(Fig. 3g-3h and Supplementary Fig. S10-S12) yield consistent conclusions, collectively
demonstrating successful synthesis of strained PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene with modulated local
electronic structure of Pd active sites.

Reaction mechanism investigations and theoretical calculations.
The adsorption behavior of EG molecules on the catalyst surface was initially investigated
using the open-circuit potential (OCP) measurements (Supplementary Fig. S26). When switching

of PdCu (0.77 V) and Pd (0.65 V), reflecting its notable affinity for EG. CO stripping experiments
reveal that the oxidation potential of the CO* intermediate on PdCuCo-0.9 is 0.77 V
(Supplementary Fig. S27), which is 20 mV and 40 mV lower than those on PdCu and Pd,
respectively, indicating the weaker CO* adsorption on PdCuCo-0.9.29 This facilitates the rapid
desorption and subsequent conversion of carbonyl (CO*) intermediates during the EGOR process,

exhibits a lower charge transfer resistance and phase angle compared to both PdCu and Pd black,

enhanced kinetic behavior can be attributed to the synergistic effects of abundant lattice defects,
metallene architecture, and multi-element alloying, which collectively accelerate the EGOR
kinetics of PdCuCo-0.9.

87.0% (D-ZEAB), confirming notable energy savings. Unlike D-ZAB, D-ZEAB prioritizes liquid
C chemicals during charging (Supplementary Fig. S37e), eliminating the formation of O and the
2 2
catalyst loss resulting from the bubble impulse, thereby extending the service life of battery. After

validating high and stable GA production efficiency in the PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB system.

of the Pt/C + Pd black reference system (763 Wh kg-1) and comparable to the recently reported
advanced ZABs, highlighting the notable energy storage performance of this catalyst (Fig. 7b and
Supplementary Table S6). Fig. 7c and Supplementary Fig. S38 show the galvanostatic
charging/discharging cycling curves of batteries at the areal discharging capacity of 5 mAh cm-2
per cycle. The PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB exhibits a narrow charging/discharging voltage gap
(∆E) of 50 mV and a high ECE of 95.7%, outperforming Pt/C+Pd black-based D-ZEAB
(Supplementary Fig. S39). Compared with the reported conventional ZABs, the PdCuCo-0.9-
based D-ZEAB is also competitive (Supplementary Table S7). In particular, only a slight decrease
of ∆E and ECE values were observed for PdCuCo-0.9 based D-ZEAB after continuous
discharging/charging for 848 cycles (a total of 1696 h), demonstrating an notable cycling stability.
Even at 10 mAh cm-2, the PdCuCo-0.9-based D-ZEAB still demonstrates an ECE of no less than
66.0% and maintains stable cycling for 615 h (Supplementary Fig. S40). Besides, the thin 2D
sheet-like morphology and defect-rich structure of PdCuCo-0.9 trimetallene after long-term
cycling tests are well preserved, verifying the structural stability (Supplementary Fig. S41 and
S42). Notably, unlike the partial oxidation of the catalyst on charging the cathode, the metallic
character and single-phase fcc structure of PdCuCo-0.9 on discharging the cathode are maintained
after long-term cycling tests (Supplementary Fig. S43 and S44). This significant difference
highlights the advantages of the spatially decoupled cathode structure of D-ZEAB in terms of
avoiding oxidation and deactivation of the ORR catalyst.

Finally, the EGOR products in the charging electrolyte of the PdCuCo-0.9 based D-ZEAB
were identified by 1H NMR spectroscopy under different cycling periods. As shown in
Supplementary Fig. S45 and S46, GA was identified as the main product during the charging
process, with trace amounts of FA by-products. The FE
GA
on the charging cathode remained above
93.0% at the areal discharging capacities of 5 and 10 mAh cm-2 per cycle, confirming the high
selectivity of GA production via PET electroreforming during the charging process of PdCuCo-
0.9 based D-ZEAB (Fig. 7d). To achieve effective resource recovery and recycling, we further
separated and purified the high-value products from the charging electrolyte after cycling tests.
Ultimately, 40.36 g TPA and 8.51 g GA were obtained from the electroreforming of 50 g PET

cost for the D-ZEAB exceeds that of a conventional ZAB by $466.7 per ton of processed PET, it

of $276.5 per ton of processed PET, confirming the D-ZEAB's economic viability (Supplementary
Tables S8-S11 and Fig. S48-S49). Notably, compared to existing aqueous zinc-based batteries
(Supplementary Table S12), the D-ZEAB proposed in this work exhibits comprehensive
superiority over critical performance metrics, including cycle life, energy conversion efficiency,
discharging capacity, and functionality, demonstrating promising application prospects.

Theoretical calculations
To investigate the performances of EGOR, DFT calculations have been performed through the
embedded CASTEP packages to understand the electronic modulations and reaction energetics in
PdCuCo catalysts.47 The generalized gradient approximation (GGAS) and Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof
(PBE) functionals were employed to describe the exchange-correlation interactions.48 The PdCuCo
alloys have been constructed based on the (111) surface of Pd in a 4×4×1 supercell with five atomic
layer thicknesses to match the experimental characterizations (Supplementary Data 1). A 20 Å
vacuum spacer was introduced along the z-axis to prevent periodic boundary effects and ensure
full relaxation. Structural optimization convergence criteria included: (1) total energy difference
<5×10-5 eV/atom, (2) maximum ionic displacement <0.005 Å, and (3) Hellmann-Feynman forces
<0.001 eV/Å.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript addresses the use of Pd-based catalysts in zinc–air batteries. The authors propose an electrocatalyst for
ethylene glycol/PET electrooxidation and oxygen reduction reactions. The innovative aspect of this work lies in the use of a
dual-cathode battery, in which the charging reaction at one of the cathodes occurs via the oxidation of ethylene glycol

to lowering energy costs, since the oxygen evolution reaction typically occurs at high overpotentials.
The manuscript is well-structured in both writing and organization of results, following a logical sequence that allows for
smooth reading and easy comprehension.The references used by the authors are current and consistent with the theme
proposed in the manuscript.
Scientifically, the electrocatalyst was characterized using key surface techniques (XRD, EDS, XPS, SVB, and XAS), while
its morphology and microstructure were examined using TEM and HAADF-STEM. The discussion of these characterization
results effectively clarifies the physical and chemical composition of the synthesized materials and how each element
contributes to the relationship between their chemical, electronic, and structural states in the studied reactions.
Regarding the analysis of reaction intermediates, the authors employed NMR and FTIR to monitor the formation of the major
species generated during the application of potential. Theoretical studies were conducted to provide a more in-depth
discussion of the energetic contributions of Cu and Co incorporated into Pd, which, to some extent, shed light on the
adsorption processes of ethylene glycol (EG) and its reaction intermediates.
However, I have some comments on the manuscript that require minor revisions so that the final work meets the necessary
standards for approval and publication in Nature Communications.
Below are my comments:
1.In my opinion, the authors should address the main motivation for studying the synthesized electrocatalyst in the
introduction. Numerous studies in the literature focus on the electrooxidation of alcohols, particularly ethylene glycol, which
is a widely studied organic molecule for various applications. The rationale for selecting a PdCuCo-based catalyst remains
unclear. A discussion of the main electrocatalysts used for this purpose could help clarify how this work advances the
frontiers of knowledge in this area.
2. Another point that caught my attention concerns the use of such a high noble-metal loading, given that the current trend is
to minimize or even eliminate the use of noble metals by replacing them with more abundant and less expensive
alternatives. Palladium is among the most expensive noble metals. Considering the practical application of the proposed
battery, would the high Pd content be commercially viable? I invite the authors to comment on this aspect.
Also, the authors compare the performance of the synthesized material with others in the literature (Figure 4f). While it is
important to highlight the performance of the material used compared to others, these comparisons often do not reflect
reality. I say this because the amount of metal (Pd) used by the authors is significant, even with normalization. Other studies
may use non-noble metals or even a reduced amount of Pd, which results in lower current densities.
3. Regarding the experiments presented, I have the following considerations:
3.1. Indicate in the figures 4(a,e) which voltammetric cycles are shown (first, second, third, etc.).
3.2. Regarding the in situ FTIR experiments, the authors used ATR-SEIRAS to analyze the intermediates formed during the
oxidation of EG. I recommend more details about the experimental procedure for obtaining the catalyst layer on the silicon
prism coated with the metal film.
I have some specific observations concerning the FTIR discussion.
The oxidation of organics on Pd is well discussed in the literature, and it is known that electrocatalytic activity depends on
the supporting electrolyte and pH. In alkaline media, bands at 1575, 14109, 1324, and 1075 cm⁻¹ can be attributed to the
formation of intermediates such as glyoxal and glycolate, which can subsequently be oxidized to glyoxylate, with the
appearance of a band at 1363 cm⁻¹ at higher potentials.
As the potential increases, a band may also appear at 1310 cm⁻¹, indicating the formation of oxalate. At high potentials,
formate can be produced, with characteristic bands at 2820, 2740, 1386, and 1353 cm⁻¹.
The carbonate ion band (1370 cm⁻¹) is typically not visible in the spectra due to overlap with the band at 1409 cm⁻¹,
although its presence can be inferred from the pronounced broadening of the latter.
It is also worth noting that glyoxal and glycolate are generally the primary products of EG electrooxidation at lower potentials.
Then, taking into accoun the above considerations about this system, the authors state that the reaction mechanism involves
the formation of glycolaldehyde; however, in alkaline media, this species is rarely identified because it tends to undergo self-
polymerization.
Regarding CO, on Pd surfaces, its formation is not easily detected in either acidic or
alkaline media. This suggests that the reaction pathway may proceed directly without CO
as an intermediate, or that CO, being only weakly adsorbed on Pd, is rapidly oxidized.
Therefore, given that the manuscript asserts the formation of CO as part of the mechanism, I encourage the authors to
reconsider whether the proposed pathway is in fact the most plausible one.

However, for the specific anodic reaction in this work, i.e., the selective electrocatalytic
oxidation of EG to GA, the current state of the art is predominantly based on noble metals
(e.g., Pd, Pt). Non-noble metal alternatives frequently suffer from insufficient selectivity
and poor stability due to C-C bond cleavage (Adv. Mater., 2024, 36, 2401867; Chinese J.
Cantal., 2025, 73, 79-98).
Our Pd-based catalyst was therefore selected to reliably establish the fundamental viability
of the integrated D-ZEAB system, achieving the high activity and selectivity required for a
robust proof-of-concept. Building on this foundation, we fully agree with the reviewer that
sustainable alternatives need to be explored. Our subsequent research will prioritize the
systematic screening of non-noble metal systems, including Co-based, Ni-based, and high-
entropy alloys, to a logical and essential next step toward scalable application (Adv. Funct.
Mater. 2024, 34, 2404594).

below.
(1) Single-cathode Zinc-ethylene Glycol/air Battery (S-ZEAB)
components (Supplementary Fig. S36): (1) A porous zinc plate anode (99.99% purity, 1.5
mm thickness); (2) a bifunctional cathode for the EGOR and ORR, fabricated by coating

(2) Dual-cathode Zinc-ethylene Glycol/air Battery (D-ZEAB)
The D-ZEAB employs a unique dual-cathode configuration comprising six key components

(2) a dedicated charging cathode for the EGOR, using a PdCuCo catalyst-loaded gas
diffusion layer; (3) a charging electrolyte of 1.0 M KOH+1.0 M EG (or PET hydrolysate);
(4) a Nafion 117 membrane, which physically separates the two cathode chambers; (5) a
dedicated discharging cathode for the ORR, also based on the PdCuCo catalyst; and (6) a
discharging electrolyte of 6.0 M KOH and 0.2 M Zn(OAc) .

7. While the electrochemical performance profiles of the PET hydrolysate and pure EG
electrolyte appear similar, what are the expected impacts of by-products and impurities on
5
the system if PET hydrolysate is used in a large-scale, high-capacity, long-term setup?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical question regarding the potential
long-term impacts of impurities in PET hydrolysate, which is essential for the practical
implementation and scalability of our D-ZEAB system.
As detailed in our composition analysis (Supplementary Fig. S20), alkaline hydrolysis of
PET (4.0 M KOH) predominantly yields EG and TPA. In this alkaline medium, the
saturation concentration of soluble TPA (or potassium terephthalate) does not exceed 0.2 M.
To assess its impact on the EGOR performance of the catalysts, we performed dedicated
electrochemical tests. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) across a TPA concentration range of 0~0.2
M shows that even at the maximum saturation concentration (0.2 M), the EGOR activity of
our PdCuCo-0.9 catalyst decreased by only ~9% (Response Fig. R1). This minor decline is
primarily attributed to a slight reduction in electrolyte pH (ΔpH≈0.5) and ionic conductivity,
which does not compromise the system’s operational integrity. Furthermore, the primary
product of EGOR on the PdCuCo-0.9 catalyst is GA, with only trace amounts of formate
detected (Supplementary Fig. S45). The long-term cycling test (Fig. 7c) confirms that these
trace by-products have a negligible impact on the charge-discharge efficiency over short-to-
medium-durations.
We fully agree, however, that in large-scale, high-capacity, long-term operation, cumulative
impurities (e.g., TPA) and by-products (e.g., formate) could potentially lead to more
significant issues, such as alterations in electrolyte composition, catalyst poisoning, or
complexities in product separation. To mitigate these for future industrial implementation,
we recommend incorporating continuous pre- and intra-process purification steps to remove
soluble contaminants. This approach would ensure sustained system stability and efficiency
over extended operational periods.

Response: We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of experimental rigor.
To ensure data accuracy and reproducibility, all battery tests adhered to the following controlled
protocols:
6
(1) Temperature control:
All electrochemical evaluations and battery tests were performed in a temperature-
controlled chamber maintained at 25 °C (±1.0 °C) to ensure thermal consistency.

To prevent irreversible capacity loss from complete zinc depletion, a strict replacement
